title: DNS
summary: Every hostname you type gets turned into an IP address before a packet moves. DNS is the global phone book that makes this work — fast, cached, and hierarchical.

blocks.markdown:
**DNS (Domain Name System)** translates human-readable hostnames like `google.com` into IP addresses like `142.250.80.46` — the format routers actually use.

- Without DNS you'd memorise IP addresses for every site.
- It is a global, distributed database with billions of records.
- It is hierarchical, delegated, and heavily cached.
- Understanding DNS explains delays, failures, and misrouting in any networked app.

blocks.subTitle: What DNS resolves
blocks.markdown:
DNS maps names to addresses (and more).

| Name | Resolved to |
|---|---|
| `google.com` | IPv4 address (A record) |
| `mail.google.com` | Mail server (MX record) |
| `www.shop.com` | Alias hostname (CNAME) |

Record types are covered in the Records section.

DNS is a tree. Authority over names is **delegated** down the tree so no single server holds everything.

- **Root** — the top of the tree (`.`). 13 root server clusters worldwide.
- **TLD (Top-Level Domain)** — `.com`, `.org`, `.in`. Each TLD has its own set of servers.
- **Authoritative server** — the server that holds the actual record for a specific domain, e.g. `google.com`.

No server knows all names; each knows its slice and who to ask next.

blocks.subTitle: Root servers
blocks.markdown:
**Root servers** are the entry point for every DNS query that cannot be answered from cache.

- There are 13 logical root server addresses (a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net).
- In practice, hundreds of physical machines handle root traffic via **anycast** (one IP, many machines, closest wins).
- Root servers do not know IP addresses — they know which TLD servers to ask next.

blocks.subTitle: TLD and authoritative servers
blocks.markdown:
Two more tiers sit below root.

- **TLD servers** know which authoritative servers are responsible for domains under their TLD. Verisign runs `.com`; ICANN delegates `.org`.
- **Authoritative name servers** hold the real records for a domain. When you buy `mysite.com`, your registrar lets you point to your own authoritative server (or use one like Cloudflare/Route 53).

A query travels: root → TLD → authoritative → answer.

A **resolver** (also called a recursive resolver or DNS client) is the middleman between your device and the DNS hierarchy.

- Your OS sends queries to a resolver — usually provided by your ISP or set manually (8.8.8.8 for Google, 1.1.1.1 for Cloudflare).
- The resolver does the legwork: it walks the hierarchy, collects the answer, caches it, and returns it to your device.
- Your device itself has a tiny local cache too — check it with `ipconfig /flushdns` or `dscacheutil -flushcache`.

blocks.subTitle: Recursive vs iterative
blocks.markdown:
There are two ways a resolver can ask for an answer.

- **Recursive** — the resolver takes on all the work. It asks root, then TLD, then authoritative, then returns the final IP to the client. Client does one query, gets one answer. Most resolvers work this way.
- **Iterative** — the server replies "I don't know, but ask this server next." The **client** loops through referrals itself. Used internally between DNS servers.

Typical flow: your device → resolver (recursive) → root/TLD/auth (iterative between servers).

Each DNS record has a **type** that says what kind of answer it holds.

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| A | Maps hostname → IPv4 address |
| AAAA | Maps hostname → IPv6 address |
| CNAME | Alias — points one hostname to another |
| MX | Mail server for a domain |
| NS | Lists the authoritative name servers |
| TXT | Free-form text; used for SPF, DKIM, domain verification |

A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name — a common gotcha.

**Caching** lets resolvers remember answers so they don't hit the full hierarchy every time.

- Each DNS record carries a **TTL (Time To Live)** — a number of seconds the answer may be cached. After TTL expires the resolver must fetch fresh data.
- A low TTL (60 s) means changes propagate quickly but traffic to authoritative servers is higher.
- A high TTL (86400 s = 1 day) reduces load but delays updates — old IPs stay cached longer.

When you migrate a server, lower the TTL days in advance.

Trace a lookup of `www.example.com` from scratch.

Seven labelled boxes in order: 'Browser' → 'OS cache (miss)' → 'Recursive Resolver' → 'Root server (returns .com TLD address)' → 'TLD server (returns authoritative NS)' → 'Authoritative server (returns A record IP)' → 'Resolver caches + returns IP' → 'Browser connects'. Arrows numbered 1-7. Label root box 'no IP known' and auth box 'holds the record'. Show cache at resolver step. >>>

1. Browser checks its own cache — miss.
2. OS resolver cache — miss. Query sent to recursive resolver.
3. Resolver asks root: "who handles .com?" → gets TLD address.
4. Resolver asks TLD: "who handles example.com?" → gets authoritative NS.
5. Resolver asks authoritative NS: "what is www.example.com?" → gets IP.
6. Resolver caches answer (respecting TTL) and returns IP.
7. Browser opens a TCP connection to that IP. See [http-https](http-https).

Traditional DNS sends queries in **plaintext UDP/TCP** — anyone on the network can see which hostnames you look up.

- **DoT (DNS over TLS)** — wraps DNS in TLS on port 853. Encrypts queries but uses a distinct port that network admins can block.
- **DoH (DNS over HTTPS)** — sends DNS queries inside HTTPS on port 443. Harder to block; used by browsers (Firefox, Chrome).

Both protect **query privacy**, not the answer's authenticity — that's what DNSSEC adds. See [network-troubleshooting-tools](network-troubleshooting-tools).

Where DNS shows up in real work:

- **CDN routing** — CDNs use DNS to return the nearest edge server's IP per-request. See [cdn-edge-caching](cdn-edge-caching).
- **Load balancing** — multiple A records for one hostname; resolvers cycle through them (round-robin DNS).
- **Health checks** — some authoritative servers remove unhealthy IPs from their records automatically.
- **Service discovery** — in Kubernetes, pods reach each other by DNS names inside the cluster.

Common mistakes:

- **"DNS changes are instant."** No — cached records live until TTL expires. Plan for propagation time.
- **"CNAME at the root domain works fine."** RFC forbids a CNAME at the zone apex (`example.com`). Use an A record or a provider's ALIAS/ANAME record instead.
- **"DNS failure is rare."** It's a frequent root cause of outages — misconfigured NS records, expired domains, and resolver timeouts all kill apps silently.

blocks.subTitle: What happens when you type a URL
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What happens at the DNS level when you type a URL and press Enter?**

Browser checks its cache → OS cache → recursive resolver. If uncached, resolver queries root → TLD → authoritative server and returns the IP. Browser then opens a TCP connection to that IP.

Best answer: mention caching at each layer and that the resolver does the hierarchy walk so the browser only makes one query.

blocks.subTitle: Recursive vs iterative
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between recursive and iterative DNS resolution?**

In **recursive** resolution the resolver does all the work and returns a final answer — the client makes one query. In **iterative** the server returns a referral ("ask this server next") and the client follows each hop itself.

In practice: your device queries a recursive resolver, which then uses iterative queries internally between DNS servers.

blocks.subTitle: A record vs CNAME
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between an A record and a CNAME?**

An **A record** maps a hostname directly to an IPv4 address. A **CNAME** maps a hostname to another hostname, which must itself eventually resolve to an A record.

Key gotcha: a CNAME cannot be placed at the zone apex (the bare domain like `example.com`) — use an A record or a provider ALIAS record there.

blocks.subTitle: Why TTL matters
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why does DNS use caching and TTL, and what trade-off does TTL control?**

Caching reduces load on authoritative servers and speeds up responses. **TTL** (Time To Live) controls how long a cached answer is trusted before the resolver re-fetches it.

Low TTL = fast propagation of changes, more server load. High TTL = fewer queries, slower updates. The right value depends on how often the record changes.

blocks.subTitle: MX record
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is an MX record and when is it used?**

An **MX (Mail Exchanger) record** specifies the mail server responsible for accepting email for a domain. When someone sends email to `user@example.com`, the sender's mail server looks up the MX record for `example.com` to find where to deliver it.

MX records also carry a **priority** number — lower is preferred, enabling failover between multiple mail servers.

blocks.subTitle: DNS and CDNs
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do CDNs use DNS to route users to the nearest edge server?**

The CDN's authoritative server inspects the resolver's IP (as a proxy for user location) and returns the IP of the nearest **edge** node. DNS becomes the routing layer — no app-level redirect needed.

This is called **anycast DNS routing** or **geo-DNS**. TTL is kept very low (seconds) so traffic shifts quickly during failures. See [cdn-edge-caching](cdn-edge-caching).
